section1_context:
bee is a Rust workspace that gives AI coding-agent tools capability-scoped access to a Linux host. Its security-critical path parses declarative policy, proves child-policy attenuation, resolves host identities and destinations, builds an eBPF-specific EnforcementPlan, attaches BPF LSM programs, creates a cgroup per scope, and enforces file-open, executable, and IP-connect decisions in the kernel. It also includes a higher-level harness for prompts, external model providers, built-in shell/file tools, local and remote MCP servers, transcripts/audit, CTF evaluation, in-process rendering, and work-in-progress SKILL.md discovery and grants.

The intended users are agent operators, framework integrators, and evaluation researchers. Production enforcement requires Linux BPF LSM/BTF/cgroup v2 and a privileged loader; the default harness build is only process-hardened and credential-stripped, not kernel-confined. The present analysis covers the dirty worktree, including uncommitted skill support. There is no database or multi-tenant service layer in this repository; the principal boundary is an untrusted or compromised model/tool workload running beneath a privileged same-host orchestrator.

section2_assets.asset: A1 — Provider API keys, MCP bearer tokens, and operator credentials
section2_assets.description: External-service authority, billing credentials, SSH/cloud secrets, and arbitrary sensitive files on the host.

section2_assets.asset: A2 — Host, harness process, and kernel enforcement integrity
section2_assets.description: Privileged orchestrator memory/environment, BPF programs/maps, cgroup membership, active LSM links, and surrounding host processes.

section2_assets.asset: A3 — Project source, artifacts, VCS metadata, and bee control-plane files
section2_assets.description: Real work product plus policy/scenario/provider/MCP/skill configuration that determines future behavior and authority.

section2_assets.asset: A4 — Sandbox policy, attenuation ceiling, executable identity, and consent decisions
section2_assets.description: The authoritative definition of allowed file, process, network, and tool capabilities.

section2_assets.asset: A5 — Network egress authority and downstream services
section2_assets.description: Model APIs, registries, remote MCP, internal endpoints, service mutations, and billable usage reachable from the host or scoped child.
section2_assets.sensitivity: Critical confidentiality, integrity, and economic value

section2_assets.asset: A6 — Prompts, model responses, tool data, skills, transcripts, metrics, and audit evidence
section2_assets.description: Potentially proprietary or secret interaction content and the evidence used to verify confinement.

section2_assets.asset: A7 — Harness availability and resource budget
section2_assets.description: CPU, memory, disk, audit capacity, provider tokens/cost, terminal state, and ability to launch confined work.

section2_assets.asset: A8 — CTF flags and evaluation/scoring integrity
section2_assets.description: Ground truth for adversarial evaluation and reproducible research results.

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E1 — CLI, environment, and host-side config/scenario materialization
section3_entry_points.description: CLI flags and TOML/YAML paths choose policies, parents, cgroup root, commands, workdirs/files, providers, endpoints, tokens, tools, skills, limits, and output paths; scenario files/directories are created before sandbox construction.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: operator or repository-controlled input -> privileged host process and filesystem

section3_entry_points.description: The harness sends prompts, tool schemas/results, and history to Anthropic or an OpenAI-compatible base URL; responses select tool names and arguments.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: local sensitive context and credential -> external provider -> tool dispatcher

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E3 — Built-in shell, process, and file tools
section3_entry_points.description: Model-controlled JSON invokes sh -c, cat, tee, ls, and other allowed binaries through either an enforced cgroup scope or host-only hardened mode.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: untrusted model output -> sandboxed child or launcher-user host authority

section3_entry_points.description: Config selects arbitrary executable/arguments/environment; the server speaks JSON-RPC and dynamically contributes tools. It is cgroup-scoped only in enforce builds.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: MCP config and third-party child process <-> harness registry/model conversation

section3_entry_points.description: A host-side client validates the authored hostname then connects using an optional bearer token; schemas, results, and list changes alter model-visible tools.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: trusted host credentials/network <-> remote server-controlled content and behavior

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E6 — Project/user skill discovery and invocation
section3_entry_points.description: Host-side code scans roots, parses YAML frontmatter, injects descriptions/bodies verbatim, applies project-over-user shadowing, and parses tool/filesystem grant requests.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: repository/user filesystem instructions -> trusted orchestrator and model behavior

section3_entry_points.description: Model-authored script is evaluated inside the harness process under explicit Rhai resource limits and a restricted drawing API.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: untrusted model script -> trusted harness address space

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E8 — Policy compilation, ambient resolution, attenuation, and planning
section3_entry_points.description: Policy input combines with cwd/HOME/PATH/DNS, protected defaults, parent-child subset logic, and fixed backend capabilities to produce map-ready rules.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: declarative authority and ambient host state -> kernel-installable policy

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E9 — Privileged loader, cgroup lifecycle, and BPF map installation
section3_entry_points.description: The host attaches global LSM hooks, creates scope cgroups, inserts map entries, moves children during pre_exec, consumes the audit map, and tears down cgroup directories.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: privileged userspace -> global kernel hooks and per-scope enforcement state

section3_entry_points.description: file_open, bprm_check_security, and socket_connect resolve runtime objects, consult cgroup-keyed maps, allow or deny, and reserve audit records.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: sandboxed process syscall -> kernel policy decision and audit stream

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E11 — Audit, transcript, metrics, and output persistence
section3_entry_points.description: Kernel records and model/tool exchanges are buffered, demultiplexed, correlated, serialized, printed, and written to operator-selected files.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: security-sensitive runtime data -> host memory/stdout/filesystem and downstream consumers

section3_entry_points.entry_point: E12 — Cargo/toolchain, GitHub Actions, and privileged VM test pipeline
section3_entry_points.description: Third-party actions, crates, rolling toolchains, bpf-linker, locally built artifacts, SSH tunnels, and sudo test runners build or validate a privileged security product.
section3_entry_points.trust_boundary: external supply chain and remote test infrastructure -> privileged release artifacts and VM root

vuln_table.title: Executable inode-pinning intent was silently downgraded to path-only enforcement
vuln_table.class: protection weakening and executable allowlist bypass
vuln_table.vector: An attacker able to replace a path-approved binary could run different code despite pin intent.

vuln_table.title: Enabled exfiltration protection was accepted but not enforced

vuln_table.entry_point: E8 — Policy compilation, ambient resolution, attenuation, and planning

vuln_table.title: Policy validation did not mean the policy was runnable
vuln_table.class: incomplete validation and fail-late control deployment
vuln_table.vector: Review or CI could approve policy intent the backend could not install.

section4_threats.threat: A host-only harness or REPL is mistaken for an enforced sandbox, so model-controlled shell/file tools run with the launcher user's ambient authority.
section4_threats.actor: untrusted or compromised model; operator making a deployment mistake
section4_threats.surface: E3 — Built-in shell, process, and file tools
section4_threats.controls: Child hardening, privileged-target refusal, output/time limits, and provider/MCP credential-name stripping; documentation notes the feature gate. These do not confine host-mode file/process/network access.

section4_threats.threat: A privileged sandbox child escapes or disables confinement by retaining root/capabilities, migrating out of its cgroup, signaling the loader, or manipulating BPF/cgroup state.
section4_threats.actor: malicious tool, dependency, or MCP stdio process launched by a privileged operator
section4_threats.surface: E9 — Privileged loader, cgroup lifecycle, and BPF map installation
section4_threats.controls: Setuid/file-capability targets are refused; core dumps, dumpability, and LD_* are hardened; pre_exec cgroup join occurs before exec. No uid/gid/capability drop or no_new_privs boundary is visible.

section4_threats.threat: Policy intent is silently weakened, omitted, or accepted despite being unenforceable, creating false assurance, unintended authority, or fail-late outages.
section4_threats.actor: malicious repository contributor or policy author; sandboxed workload exploiting an intent/enforcement gap
section4_threats.surface: E8 — Policy compilation, ambient resolution, attenuation, and planning
section4_threats.controls: Two-stage CompiledPolicy -> EnforcementPlan; unsupported capabilities and capacity overflow reject before Engine/cgroup state; attenuation checks; CLI validate plans the effective policy; planner/CLI/VM regression tests.

section4_threats.threat: Operations outside the attached LSM hooks or helper error paths bypass intended file, exec, or egress restrictions.
section4_threats.controls: Kernel-resolved file paths, cgroup-keyed enforcement, fail-closed support/offset gates, and file_open/bprm_check_security/socket_connect hooks. Rename/link/unlink, inherited descriptors, UDP sendto, non-IP sockets, hard-link/bind-mount aliases, and several helper failures remain outside or allow.

section4_threats.threat: Repository-controlled scenario/provider configuration performs privileged parent-side writes or selects an arbitrary environment secret and sends it to an attacker-controlled model endpoint before sandboxing.
section4_threats.surface: E1 — CLI, environment, and host-side config/scenario materialization
section4_threats.controls: Typed parsing and some semantic validation; provider files store env-var names rather than literal keys. Workdir materialization is host-side and base_url/api_key_env remain config-controlled.

section4_threats.threat: Remote MCP hostname gating is crossed through redirects, DNS rebinding/private resolution, URL-parser differences, or a compromised allowed server; bearer tokens and model decisions are then exposed or manipulated.
section4_threats.actor: malicious remote MCP operator, DNS/network attacker, or repository config author
section4_threats.controls: Remote MCP defaults disabled, empty allowlist denies, exact/wildcard hostname rules and deny precedence, TLS defaults, token names rather than values, timeouts and server caps. Only the authored initial hostname is visibly gated.

section4_threats.threat: An arbitrary or compromised MCP stdio binary runs unconfined in host mode or receives explicitly reintroduced sensitive environment values, then influences dynamically registered tools/results.
section4_threats.actor: malicious repository config author or compromised MCP package/binary
section4_threats.controls: Enforce builds use the same cgroup-join/hardening path as built-in tools; credential env names are stripped and tool filtering exists. Host mode has no kernel confinement and explicit config env is added after command construction.

section4_threats.threat: A compromised crate, action, rolling toolchain, bpf-linker package, or MITM'd VM test endpoint substitutes a privileged userspace/BPF artifact.
section4_threats.actor: supply-chain maintainer compromise, registry/GitHub attacker, or network/control-plane attacker
section4_threats.surface: E12 — Cargo/toolchain, GitHub Actions, and privileged VM test pipeline
section4_threats.controls: Rust lock resolution is present locally, code review, fmt/clippy/tests, kernel verifier, and VM matrix. Third-party actions/toolchains are mutable, bpf-linker is unversioned, relevant lockfiles are untracked, and SSH host-key verification is disabled in the VM tunnel.

section4_threats.threat: A malicious project or shadowing skill injects trusted-looking instructions that steer tool use, solicit secrets, or induce operator approval of capability grants.
section4_threats.actor: malicious repository contributor or compromised user skill source
section4_threats.surface: E6 — Project/user skill discovery and invocation
section4_threats.controls: Model-invocation flags, deterministic precedence, parse warnings, capability ceiling, consent abstraction, and non-interactive DenyAll. Bodies/descriptions are injected verbatim host-side; provenance/signing is absent and grant wiring is work in progress.

section4_threats.threat: An external model provider, malicious compatible base URL, or provider account compromise discloses prompts, source/tool output, flags, or returns adversarial tool calls while consuming unbounded billable capacity.
section4_threats.actor: provider operator/compromise, network attacker within TLS trust, or config author
section4_threats.controls: TLS/provider library, turn/time/token settings, retry classification, tool registry, sandbox enforcement when enabled, and credential stripping from children. Conversation disclosure to the selected provider is inherent.

section4_threats.threat: PATH, HOME, project-root, or DNS state changes between policy preparation and use cause executable/path/destination identity to drift from what the operator reviewed.
section4_threats.actor: local attacker controlling ambient resolution or allowed DNS; compromised dependency modifying paths
section4_threats.surface: E8 — Policy compilation, ambient resolution, attenuation, and planning
section4_threats.controls: Names resolve before planning; impossible resolutions reject; LSM resolves actual file paths; inode pinning requests reject rather than weaken. Runtime DNS refresh and inode-pinned executable enforcement are not implemented.

section4_threats.threat: Partial scope installation or stale cgroup-keyed BPF entries survive failures/teardown and later misapply old rules after cgroup-ID reuse or exhaust map capacity.
section4_threats.actor: malicious workload inducing churn/failures; ordinary long-running concurrent use
section4_threats.surface: E9 — Privileged loader, cgroup lifecycle, and BPF map installation
section4_threats.controls: Planning precedes kernel mutation and scope teardown removes the cgroup directory. No transactional rollback or removal of SCOPES/FS/EXEC/NET entries is visible.

section4_threats.threat: Transcripts, metrics, audit targets, or operator-selected output paths disclose secrets or are overwritten/tampered with, undermining privacy and evaluation evidence.
section4_threats.actor: local user/process, malicious scenario/model content, or careless operator
section4_threats.surface: E11 — Audit, transcript, metrics, and output persistence
section4_threats.controls: Per-tool output truncation and structured serialization. Records still contain full assistant text, tool arguments/results, paths, identifiers, and timing; no redaction, restrictive-create mode, encryption, retention, or integrity control is visible.

section4_threats.threat: Audit ring overflow, silent reservation failure, or unbounded concurrent subscriber queues lose denial evidence or exhaust harness memory.
section4_threats.surface: E11 — Audit, transcript, metrics, and output persistence
section4_threats.controls: Fixed-size kernel ring, cgroup-based demultiplexing, per-call drain and re-filtering. Ring reserve failure drops records and userspace subscriber channels are unbounded.

section4_threats.threat: Model-authored Rhai exploits an interpreter/API bug or pathological computation inside the trusted harness process, causing code execution, memory corruption, or denial of service outside the kernel scope.
section4_threats.controls: Opt-in tool, restricted registered API, eval disabled, and operation/call/expression/string/array/map/render caps. It still evaluates attacker-authored code in-process and depends on interpreter correctness.

section4_threats.threat: The enforcement path regresses without detection because CI treats the enforce check as best-effort and live BPF-LSM behavior remains a manual external-VM gate.
section4_threats.actor: ordinary developer error or malicious contributor exploiting test gaps
section4_threats.surface: E12 — Cargo/toolchain, GitHub Actions, and privileged VM test pipeline
section4_threats.controls: Host unit/property/integration tests and a documented VM matrix exist. The enforcement CI job is continue-on-error and does not execute the live matrix.

section4_threats.threat: Documented broad filesystem semantics—unmatched reads, some unmatched writes, observe mode, and name-based path aliases—are misunderstood as deny-by-default confinement and expose project or host data.
section4_threats.actor: operator misconfiguration combined with malicious sandboxed process
section4_threats.controls: Policy contract, README caveats, protected defaults for .git/.bee/.ssh/.aws, write-default flag, and explicit observe mode. The top-level zero-capabilities wording can still overstate actual read semantics.

section5_deprioritized.threat: Database injection and record-level authorization failures
section5_deprioritized.reason: No database, ORM, or query interface exists in the reviewed repository.

section5_deprioritized.threat: Browser-origin CSRF, XSS, and session fixation
section5_deprioritized.reason: No browser-served application or cookie-authenticated web UI is present.
bee is primarily a local CLI/library/harness; outbound model/MCP connections are covered instead.

section5_deprioritized.threat: Kubernetes/IAM lateral identity and residual cloud grants
section5_deprioritized.reason: No Kubernetes, Terraform, cloud IAM, service-account, or dataset ACL configuration is managed in this tree; privileged local/VM identities are covered under E9/E12.
The repository models a local operator and scoped workloads rather than mutually distrusting application users. Audit integrity/completeness is covered separately.

mitigation_notes.recommended_mitigation: Make all model-executing entry points refuse untrusted workloads unless enforcement is compiled and active; require an explicit, loudly recorded unsafe-host-mode opt-in.
Split the privileged loader from an unprivileged runner and drop uid/gid, capabilities, supplementary groups, and privilege regain before executing workload code; prevent cgroup migration.
Require an executable policy-conformance matrix for every documented capability/mode at the kernel boundary; reject representations with no enforcing backend and gate releases on the live matrix.

mitigation_notes.cluster: LSM coverage gaps and broad semantics
mitigation_notes.recommended_mitigation: Define and test an explicit syscall/descriptor threat contract, add missing hooks or complementary mechanisms for metadata operations and connectionless/inherited I/O, and fail closed on helper-resolution errors where safe.
Treat repository provider/scenario files as untrusted: constrain materialization/output beneath an approved root and require operator approval for nonstandard base URLs and secret env-var names.
Resolve and pin allowed public addresses, reject private/loopback/link-local results, revalidate every redirect/connection, and isolate remote MCP content/credentials behind a least-privilege broker.
Disable stdio MCP in host mode, validate added env keys against a secret denylist, and require executable identity pinning or trusted installation provenance.
Commit lockfiles, pin actions/toolchains/bpf-linker by immutable digest/version, verify artifacts, enable SSH host verification, and make the live BPF matrix a required protected-branch release gate.
Display source and requested deltas at invocation, bind grants to reviewed content hashes, prevent silent shadowing, and keep capability activation separate from instruction loading.
Allowlist provider origins and credential env names at an operator-controlled layer; redact/classify outbound context and enforce spend/data-retention policy.
Bind policy rules to stable executable/file identities and continuously refresh/revalidate DNS destinations with private-range protections.
Make scope creation transactional with rollback and remove every per-cgroup map entry before cgroup teardown; test cgroup-ID reuse and churn.
Redact secrets, create outputs with restrictive permissions, define retention/integrity controls, bound audit queues, and surface dropped-event counters as enforcement-health failures.
Move model-authored rendering into a separate unprivileged, resource-limited process with a narrow serialized RenderSpec interface.

locations: bee-harness/src/bin/bee-repl.rs: non-enforce build ignores supplied policy
bee-harness/src/episode.rs: default host sandbox has no kernel policy
bee-harness/src/skills.rs and skills/grant.rs: requires/grant semantics are split across discovery and later wiring
bee-harness/src/mcp/config.rs: tool allow/deny filters are explicitly not a security boundary
